content: The introduction of complementary feeding during the early years of life is critical for establishing and maintaining the nutritional health of infants. Failure to introduce complementary foods between 6 and 23 months of age can result in malnutrition. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends including a variety of complementary foods such as fruits and vegetables, animal-source foods (ASF), and nuts, pulses, and seeds to meet the nutritional needs of infants during this period of rapid growth and development. Among these, animal-source foods are particularly important as they are rich in both macroand micronutrients, provide high-quality proteins, and stimulate growth-promoting hormones in children. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the health, developmental, and dietary effects of more frequent versus less frequent, greater versus lesser amounts, and more varied versus less varied consumption of animal-source foods during the complementary feeding period. Additionally, the review sought to compare the effects of processed/commercial versus fresh/home-prepared animal-source foods on dietary and health outcomes. The search strategy for this review was developed using the PICO methodology and included searches in electronic databases such as MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, African Index Medicus, LILACS, Cochrane CENTRAL, and eLENA (WHO). Grey literature was also reviewed using Google Scholar, organizational websites, and reference lists of relevant systematic reviews. All search results were screened in duplicate, and individual studies were critically appraised using tools such as the Cochrane Risk of Bias-2 (ROB-2) tool for randomized controlled trials, the NIH tool for observational studies, and the ROBINS-I tool for non-randomized studies. The GRADE approach was used to assess the certainty of evidence for outcomes included in meta-analyses, such as stunting, wasting, underweight, changes in head circumference, triceps skinfold thickness, and anemia or hemoglobin levels. The review included 31 studies involving data from 278,358 children aged 0–12 years at enrollment. These studies were conducted in various regions, including Europe, Africa, Asia, North America, South America, and one multi-center study. Of the included studies, 17 were observational, 15 were randomized experimental studies, and one was a non-randomized experimental study. Thirteen studies examined the frequency of ASF consumption, 18 assessed the amount of ASF consumed, and two evaluated the variety of ASF consumed. However, most outcomes were reported by single studies, limiting the ability to draw definitive conclusions about the effects of different frequencies, amounts, and varieties of ASF consumption. Regarding the frequency of ASF consumption, no randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs were identified. Observational studies showed no significant differences in outcomes between greater and lesser amounts of ASF consumption, except for a 48% reduction in wasting among children who consumed fish four or more times per week compared to those who consumed fish 1–3 times per week (GRADE: moderate). For the amount of ASF consumed, no significant differences in growth and nutritional outcomes were observed among children given different types of meat, including red meat, organ meat, pork, eggs, dairy, seafood, and insects. These studies involved children aged 6–9 months who were followed for six months after being given one egg per day versus no egg consumption (GRADE: moderate to low quality). Regarding the variety of ASF consumed, no RCTs or quasi-RCTs were identified. Observational studies reported no significant differences in stunting among children consuming three types of ASF versus two types, or two types versus one type. However, a potential 1% reduction in stunting was observed in children consuming one type of ASF compared to those consuming none (GRADE: very low). Overall, the quality of observational studies was rated as good for two studies, fair for nine studies, and poor for six studies. Among randomized experimental studies, one was rated as high risk of bias, nine as moderate risk, and three as low risk. The single non-randomized experimental study was rated as low to moderate risk of bias. The findings of this systematic review aim to inform the development of updated WHO guidelines on infant and young child feeding, as well as country-specific policies and programs related to complementary feeding. However, the high heterogeneity among studies limited the ability to conduct meta-analyses for most outcomes. Only three outcomes (WAZ, HAZ, WHZ) from two studies were meta-analyzed, with a GRADE rating of low to moderate. This review highlights significant gaps in evidence and study quality, underscoring the need for more consistent and higher-quality research to enable pooled findings and the development of appropriate guidelines. Adequate nutrition during infancy is essential for a child’s physical and cognitive development. The first two years of life are a critical period for growth, during which poor dietary intake and diseases can have long-term consequences, including impaired intellectual performance, reduced work capacity, and poor reproductive and overall health outcomes. Complementary feeding, initiated at six months of age alongside breastfeeding, is crucial to meet the increasing nutritional demands of growing infants. Animal-source foods, in particular, are rich in nutrients such as vitamin A, vitamin B12, calcium, zinc, iron, and riboflavin, which are not adequately provided by plant-based foods alone. Insufficient intake of these nutrients can lead to anemia, growth abnormalities, cognitive decline, and other health issues. Despite the importance of ASF, many parents avoid giving these foods to their children due to concerns about digestion, cultural or religious beliefs, lack of awareness, or the high cost of ASF products. This review emphasizes the need for educational interventions to improve complementary feeding practices and highlights the potential benefits of including ASF in the diets of infants and young children. Findings from this review will contribute to the development of updated WHO guidelines and future policies to improve the health and well-being of infants, with lasting effects throughout their lives.
